strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful problem: predicting human response times under changing external feedback. Combining task-derived neural features with an evidence-accumulation model and learned modulation is a plausible, potentially useful approach.

The two-day behavioral study provides substantial repeated measurements across four feedback conditions, with 36 participants retained for analysis. Evaluation includes individual, group, pooled, and leave-one-participant-out settings, providing useful evidence beyond a single random split.

The hybrid model reports lower aggregate MAPE than Pure DRL in all four settings and substantially shorter training time on the same hardware: 4.42 versus 38.30 minutes. The feature-representation comparison also supports using arithmetic-task representations for behavioral prediction.
weaknesses: Essential methods are missing from the supplied manuscript. Referenced Appendices S2–S6 are absent, leaving the RL algorithm, reward, evidence-accumulation equations, diffusion parameters, adaptive-feedback rule, and important training details unspecified. The mapping from SVM predictions to diffusion dynamics is particularly important for assessing the model's validity. Code and data are promised without an accessible release. These omissions prevent reproduction and verification of the central contribution.

The comparisons do not isolate the proposed combination's contribution. Pure DRL removes both the diffusion model and frame-by-frame processing, so its comparison confounds multiple design choices. Stimulus-aware supervised predictors, a time-dependent DDM, and ablations replacing visual frames with elapsed time or stimulus presence would provide stronger tests. Although earlier neural/cognitive and RL–DDM hybrids are cited, the advance over these approaches remains insufficiently established. The assertion that DDM is limited to posterior estimation also understates its predictive capabilities.

The cognitive interpretation exceeds the evidence. Multiple action trajectories can yield the same boundary-crossing time, so accurate response-time prediction does not identify the underlying human accumulation process. Reproducing group patterns from the behavioral dataset is not independent validation of that mechanism. Nonzero 'time pressure effect' trajectories also appear in the no-pressure condition, suggesting that actions may partly compensate for baseline prediction errors. Controlled changes to stimulus timing or predictions under unseen temporal schedules would better test the central frame-level claim.

The predictive gains require stronger uncertainty analysis. General-level MAPE improves from 0.3034 to 0.2999, and leave-one-participant-out MAPE from 0.3037 to 0.2905—approximately 1.2% and 4.3% relative improvements. Participant-level paired confidence intervals and repeated training runs are needed to establish robustness. It is also unclear whether SVM fitting, normalization, and model selection exclude each held-out participant throughout the complete pipeline. The training-time comparison lacks an explicit, reproducible convergence criterion.

The behavioral conclusions should be narrower. The final groups contain only 7–10 participants, and three participants were excluded as extreme outliers without a stated criterion or sensitivity analysis. The reported significant response-time comparison is between random and no feedback; this does not establish that random feedback outperforms static or adaptive feedback. The proposed explanation involving habituation is plausible but untested. Together with the methodological and validation gaps, these concerns outweigh the promising initial results.
